summary:
Castilla-La Mancha stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities, including this one, and the source inventory identifies no facility, expression or assembly restriction enacted at regional level.

Document-relevant provision is national and administrative. Adults may request rectification of the sex entry on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, without prior surgical reassignment, a gender-dysphoria diagnosis or two years of medical treatment; the right is grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious during passage.

Because access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, that registry entry is the operative basis for facility rules in Castilla-La Mancha, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

The national statute defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the covered causes, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances. Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) recorded that the law strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Other operative provisions of the national statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, and strengthened sexuality education. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.
tangentialFactors:
The two enforcement examples cited, Vigo and Valencia, are drawn from Galicia and the Valencian Community respectively; they illustrate how the national aggravating circumstance is applied by Spanish courts but do not evidence any Castilla-La Mancha-specific proceeding.

Spain's administrative self-declaration regime is comparatively permissive: it sits alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in permitting legal gender change without diagnosis, surgery or sterilisation. The United Kingdom's movement toward a biological-sex-based single-sex-spaces framework marks the principal regional divergence a visitor may notice when crossing between the two jurisdictions.

The 2016 23-country survey ranking Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed predates Ley 4/2023 by seven years and should be read as a baseline rather than a current measurement.
